Clean, angular washed gravel (commonly 3/4 in.) placed around the perforated pipe, wrapped in filter fabric to keep Oregon's silty clay from clogging the system over time — a real, Oregon-soil-specific detail sourced from a contractor blog, not fabricated

Geotextile fabric wrapping the gravel/pipe assembly to prevent fine soil particles from migrating into and clogging the drain over time — a genuine failure-point education opportunity (a French drain installed without fabric in Willamette Valley clay silts up faster)

A grated inlet box set at a low point to collect surface water and route it into a buried pipe system — distinct from a French drain (which intercepts water along a trench) and named directly by M4 Landworks and the current live D&D page, but not defined or explained by any competitor

An underground chamber that collects a volume of water and slowly releases it back into the surrounding soil via infiltration — functionally different from a French drain (which conveys water continuously to an exit point) and often paired with one (French drain discharges INTO a dry well) rather than substituting for it. canonical_name: City of Eugene Stormwater Connection Permit (EC 6.610)
notes: VERIFIED 2026-09-09: Eugene Code §6.610 — no person may connect a drain, downspout, or other conduit carrying stormwater to the city stormwater system without paying required fees and obtaining a permit from the City Engineer, issued only upon a determination the connection is a proper use of the system. Permits are issued only to a property owner (for their own residence) or to a licensed plumber/licensed septic-tank-installation contractor — a real, specific, checkable restriction on WHO can even pull this permit. Lines connecting private catch basins/pipes into the city system are not a city maintenance responsibility once connected. This is the single most concrete, uncontested Oregon-specific authority signal available to this page
